Section 01

Exhibit Introduction and Overview

The riot grrl movement is central to the American female experience because it spread the third wave of feminism to the younger generation and music scene by pushing more women to realize they are not alone in their struggles with their gender roles. Punk music was a way for all girls to have a way of releasing their frustrations through punk music just like men have had for many years by pushing back against patriarchy in a male-dominated space, and it created a type of punk that directly empowered women instead of just men.



Why Riot Grrrl Matters in Broader Context of Women's History
Brought third-wave feminist issues (patriarchy, gender equality)to younger generations of women
Punk music gave teenage girls a creative outlet to push back against male-dominated spaces
One of the rare moments in women's history where younger and older generations actively collaborated in the same movement
Complemented the Anita Hill hearings (1991), amplifying the third-wave feminist movement
Empowered girls to take up space in punk rock music, which had historically excluded or marginalized them
Zines, self-published booklets, wrote about feminist issues and brought communication and community to the movement
Legacy continues today through online platforms, proving its ideas remain relevant to ongoing fights for gender equality and LGBTQ+ rights

Section 02

Timeline

1970s
Women Enter Punk
Patti Smith, Siouxsie Sioux, and The Slits lay groundwork for women in punk. Despite their influence, women remain marginalized in the broader punk movement.
1991
Riot Grrrl Is Born and Goes National
Bratmobile forms at a DC punk show. Riot Grrrl zine published. Erin Smith tips off Sassy magazine, leading to its first mainstream coverage. Anita Hill hearings ignite third wave feminism.
1992
The Manifesto and "Year of Riot Grrrl"
Olympia meetings plan a coordinated "girl riot." Riot Grrrl Manifesto published. National media coverage explodes across the country.
1997
Bikini Kill Disbands
The most prominent Riot Grrrl band disbands, marking the end of the movement's peak era.
2000
Seattle: EMP Opening and The White Stripes
Bratmobile plays the EMP opening. The White Stripes open for them in December. Jack White tries to buy Erin's vintage guitar. She declines.
2023
Rolling Stone: Erin Smith #240
Rolling Stone names Erin Smith the 240th greatest guitarist of all time, recognition that "never would've happened in the 90s."
2024
Smithsonian Virtual Museum Launches
The Smithsonian American Women's History Museum launches its first digital exhibition, cementing the movement's historical legacy.
01
Artifact 01 of 05
Written Document

Riot Grrrl Manifesto

Author: Kathleen Hanna / Bikini Kill
Title: Riot Grrrl Manifesto
Published in zine format - Olympia, Washington - 1992
Archived: History Is a Weapon (historyisaweapon.com)
The Riot Grrrl Manifesto is one of the foundational documents of the movement, written in the raw, urgent voice of the zines that gave Riot Grrrl its identity. It articulates precisely why these bands existed and what they were fighting against. The manifesto pushes back against the expectation that women must assimilate to male standards, stating: "BECAUSE us girls crave records and books and fanzines that speak to US." Punk rock was designed to express anger, but the anger of boys. Girls had their own anger, their own problems, and their own stories. This document insisted those stories deserved a stage. The manifesto is also a direct product of the third wave of feminism: it rejects the idea that equality means sameness, instead demanding space for the specifically female experience within punk culture. It remains one of the clearest statements of what Riot Grrrl was, and why it mattered.
02
Artifact 02 of 05
Material Object - Visual Artifact

"Start A Riot" Flyer

Author: Unknown
Title: Start A Fucking Riot
Location: Unknown - c. Early 1990s
Source: Yale Review Riot Grrrl Archive (yalereview.org)
This flyer describes steps to start a riot grrl chapter. It mentions finding supporters, having frequent meetings, creating flyers and zines, and communicating with other riot grrl movements and bands (the last point is especially emphasized). Aimed at teenage girls, this poster shows that the riot grrl movement was not just trying to get young girls to attend riot grrl shows, but also to get girls to start their own movements. The riot grrl movement's focus on the younger generation is a key strategy for social change; they likely learned from the civil rights movement's focus on college students through the SNCC organization.
03
Artifact 03 of 05
Material Object - Archival Collection

The Riot Grrrl Collection

Authors: Various
Title: The Riot Grrrl Collection
Olympia, Washington and Washington, D.C. - 1991 to 1994
Archived: Fales Library and Special Collections, New York University
The Riot Grrrl Collection is a collection of zines that were a feminist response to sexism in punk culture and music. These zines encouraged girls to create bands and tell their story and get their message out into the world through the mechanism of punk music and DIY culture. These zines were never supposed to be perfect and neat. Instead, these zines were raw, handmade, and intentionally homemade in feeling. They mixed diary entries, political essays, drawings, manifestos, poetry, collages, and any other art form. These zines specifically made music easier to approach by emphasizing that you don't have to be an expert musician to spread your message and share your story. Overall, these zines encouraged girls to embrace their stories, spread feminism, and resist sexism in a tangible way.
04
Artifact 04 of 05
Primary Source - Individual Spotlight

Interview with Erin Smith

Subject: Erin Smith, co-founder and guitarist of Bratmobile
Conducted by: Jonah, Federal Way, Washington
Format: Email interview - May 15 to 18, 2026
This primary source interview captures the firsthand account of Erin Smith, co-founder and guitarist of Bratmobile. Smith describes how the band formed organically, meeting her future bandmates at a DC punk show over Christmas break, and how she entered a music scene where women were broadly unwelcome. She recalls boys asking whose guitar she was carrying at school, as if it couldn't possibly be hers: a small but telling detail of the cultural barriers women faced. Smith also reveals her direct role in bringing Riot Grrrl to national attention, having personally told Sassy magazine about the movement during her 1991 internship, leading to its first mainstream coverage. Conducted over three decades after Bratmobile's formation, the interview demonstrates the movement's urgency has not faded. As Smith put it: "there's a new 14-year-old girl every day that needs to hear our music."
05
Artifact 05 of 05
Material Object

Erin Smith's Vintage Guitar

Owner: Erin Smith, Bratmobile - Private collection
Type: Vintage electric guitar - c. Early 1990s
Photograph courtesy of Erin Smith
This guitar is more than an instrument; it is a declaration. When Erin Smith picked it up in the early 1990s and helped form Bratmobile, she was entering a punk scene that, as she describes it, women "did not generally feel included in." She was unconcerned with technical perfection or meeting male-defined standards of musicianship, stating simply that she "had music to get out." That refusal to seek approval was central to Riot Grrrl's ethos. In December 2000, Jack White, then an emerging guitarist who would become one of rock's most celebrated, offered to buy this guitar from Smith after Bratmobile headlined a Seattle show he opened. She declined. In 2023, Rolling Stone named Smith the 240th greatest guitarist of all time, a recognition that affirms what Riot Grrrl always argued: women belonged in rock. They always did.

01 / 08

Full Interview: Erin Smith, Bratmobile - May 2026

Email interview - May 15 to 18, 2026 - Conducted by Jonah, Federal Way, Washington
How and why did Bratmobile form, and what was happening in the broader cultural and political landscape for women that made a band like yours feel necessary at that moment?
My 2 bandmates were going to college in Oregon and I was at University of Maryland. When one of them came home to DC for Christmas, we were introduced by a mutual friend at a punk show. Later, when both of them came to visit DC for spring break, they'd already heard through the grapevine that I was playing guitar and writing songs and asked if I wanted to jam. The rest is history!

In a broader sense, while we were certainly not the first all-girl punk band, punk was a very male movement that women did not generally feel included in at that time. Somebody had to do it, why not us? I never cared about being Eric Clapton or "perfect" - I just had music that I wanted to get out there and felt I had something to offer.
Riot Grrrl is often described as both a music movement and a feminist political movement. How did you see those two things intersecting in your work?
We were a band before the movement had a name. Riot Grrrl really just started out as a fanzine put together by members of Bratmobile, Bikini Kill, and some other women, sharing thoughts about feminism and just everyday life in the punk scene. Only after the fanzine came out did people start referring to our bands as "Riot Grrrl" bands. I was interning at Sassy magazine in New York for part of the Summer of 1991 and I told them about the 'Zine Riot Grrrl. Sassy became the first mainstream publication to write about Riot Grrrl and word spread from there and kind of ballooned after that.
Are there specific objects, zines, flyers, or recordings from Bratmobile's history that you feel are especially important to preserve or represent? Why?
I'm a real historian, so I think all of those objects are valuable to preserve. Physical media is having a real resurgence right now, but things like 'zines and flyers are rarer these days with most of those things online now. I don't believe in streaming at all personally, so the physical LPs, CDs, and cassettes are invaluable to me. We all lose as far as looking back on history when there is no physical object to look at!
How do you think the issues Bratmobile addressed in the early 90s connect to what young women and girls are navigating today?
I have always said that there's a new 14-year-old girl every day that needs to hear our music. The themes are universal and none of the issues have gone away!
What do you think is most misunderstood or left out of how Riot Grrrl and Bratmobile get talked about in mainstream music history?
I think just that we were dismissed as being amateurish. Who cares if that's true? To me some of the more technically "perfect" music has no soul, and "amateurish" minimalist punk music means the most to me!
Is there anything else you'd like us to know?
In 2023, Rolling Stone Magazine named me the number 240 greatest guitarist of all time, out of 250. It's a huge honor, and with a number like 240, you know I'm not making that up! This never would've happened in the 90s - it's only in retrospect that publications like Rolling Stone are taking another look at giving women their due.

Since you're in high school, I can share that when I'd carry my guitar case at school, boys used to ask me, "Whose guitar is that??" as if it couldn't be mine! I feel like I've heard Taylor Swift tell a similar story. I can only hope that with more all-girl bands like mine and all that have come since, it becomes more and more normal to expect a girl might be carrying her own guitar.

The White Stripes opened for us in Seattle in December, 2000. This wasn't unusual at the time since they were the much smaller band in 2000, but it seems wild to think of it now. Jack White asked if he could buy my very rare vintage guitar. Of course I said no!
